subject: zoology
question_text: List out the major air pollutants and describe their effects on human beings.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.28, LAQ 12). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. RULE 35 (globally neutral content): the book's acid rain line cites the Taj Mahal by name as the monument damaged. This card writes the effect in general terms instead — 'buildings and monuments made of marble and limestone' — which states WHY the stone is attacked and keeps the answer portable across syllabi. A student who writes the Taj Mahal is not wrong. BOOK POSITION: the book lists 'Noise pollution' as the sixth major AIR pollutant. Noise is strictly a separate kind of pollution and not a chemical constituent of the air; it is answered here because the board's expected answer for this question lists it, and the point is recorded in that step's why field.

steps.label: Air pollution and the list
lines: Air pollution: any deviation from the
natural composition of the air that causes
adverse effects to humans and plants is
called air pollution.
The agents that carry air pollution are
called air pollutants.
Major air pollutants:
1) Carbon monoxide (CO)
2) Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
3) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂)
4) Nitrogen oxides (NO, N₂O, NO₂)
5) Aerosols (particulate matter)
6) Noise pollution
steps.why: The question says list out first, so the six names are written as a numbered list before any of them is described; the list is worth two marks on its own and also becomes the order of the rest of the answer.
common_mistakes: Describing the pollutants without listing them first. The list is asked for by name.
Leaving out the definition of air pollution, which opens the answer.
Naming chlorofluorocarbons. They are not in this book's list of six.
steps.memory_tip: Two carbon gases, one sulphur gas, the nitrogen oxides, the particles and the noise. Six items.
steps.margin_note: Definition in two sentences, then the six names as a numbered list. Two marks.

steps.label: Carbon monoxide
lines: Carbon monoxide (CO) is produced by the
incomplete combustion of fossil fuels.
Sources: automobile exhausts, factory fumes,
emissions from power plants, forest fires
and the burning of fire wood.
Harmful effects:
i) In the presence of carbon monoxide the
oxygen carrying capacity of haemoglobin is
reduced.
ii) At lower concentrations it causes
headache and blurred vision.
iii) At higher concentrations it leads to
coma and sometimes to death.
Every pollutant below follows the same
order: source, then harmful effects.
steps.why: Carbon monoxide acts on one target only, the haemoglobin, so that fact is written first and the two levels of effect follow from it in order of dose — mild at low concentration, fatal at high.
common_mistakes: Writing that carbon monoxide comes from complete combustion. It comes from INCOMPLETE combustion.
Writing that it damages the lungs. It acts on the HAEMOGLOBIN of the blood.
Giving the effects without separating the low and high concentrations.
steps.memory_tip: Carbon monoxide takes the seat oxygen should have on the haemoglobin. Low dose: headache. High dose: coma.
steps.margin_note: Source line, then three effects in order of dose. Keep the same shape for all six pollutants.

steps.label: Carbon dioxide
lines: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is produced by the
respiration of living beings, but plants use
it for photosynthesis.
Sources: burning of fossil fuels such as
gasoline, automobiles, aeroplanes and power
plants.
Harmful effects:
i) When its concentration rises above the
normal level it results in global warming.
ii) Global warming brings many adverse
effects on mankind, such as climatic change
and the melting of the polar ice.
steps.why: Carbon dioxide is the one pollutant on the list that is also a normal part of the air, so the answer says plants use it before saying it is harmful — the harm is in the EXCESS, not in the gas.
common_mistakes: Writing that carbon dioxide is poisonous like carbon monoxide. Its harm is global warming, not poisoning.
Leaving out the words above the normal level. Ordinary carbon dioxide is not a pollutant.
steps.memory_tip: Carbon monoxide poisons the blood; carbon dioxide warms the planet. One letter, two different harms.
steps.margin_note: Note that plants use it, then the sources, then global warming as the effect.

steps.label: Sulphur dioxide
lines: Sulphur dioxide (SO₂) is produced mainly by
the burning of fossil fuels, the melting of
sulphur ores and metal smelting.
Harmful effects:
i) Breathing problems such as asthma.
ii) Aggravation of cardiovascular problems.
iii) Corrosion of buildings and monuments.
steps.why: Sulphur dioxide is the pollutant whose effects reach both people and stone, so the three effects are written to cover the lungs, the heart and the buildings.
common_mistakes: Writing that sulphur dioxide causes global warming. That is carbon dioxide.
Giving only the effects on people. The corrosion of buildings is one of the three.
steps.memory_tip: Sulphur dioxide attacks two things: the breathing passages and the stone of buildings.
steps.margin_note: Source line, then three effects. Keep this one short; it is a single mark.

steps.label: Nitrogen oxides
lines: Nitrogen oxides (NO, N₂O, NO₂) are produced
by automobile exhaust.
Harmful effects:
i) The oxides of nitrogen together with
sulphur dioxide produce acid rain.
ii) Acid rain acidifies water bodies and
spoils crops, buildings and monuments made
of marble and limestone.
iii) Nitrogen dioxide with hydrocarbons and
sunlight in foggy conditions produces
photochemical smog. Spots form on leaves,
photosynthesis is reduced and the crop
yield falls.
iv) Nitrogen oxides combine with secondary
pollutants to form PAN (peroxy acetyl
nitrate), which irritates the eyes and the
respiratory tract.
steps.why: The nitrogen oxides are the busiest pollutant on the list because they produce three named products — acid rain, photochemical smog and PAN — and each of those has to be named, since the marks are given for the names.
common_mistakes: Writing that nitrogen oxides alone make acid rain. Sulphur dioxide acts together with them.
Leaving out PAN. Its full name, peroxy acetyl nitrate, is the one the examiner looks for.
Leaving out photochemical smog, which needs sunlight and fog together with the hydrocarbons.
steps.memory_tip: Three products from one family: acid rain, photochemical smog and PAN.
steps.margin_note: Name all three products in full. This mark is dense, so use short numbered lines.

steps.label: Aerosols
lines: Aerosols, also called particulate matter,
are colloidal particles dispersed in a gas.
Sources: combustion of fossil fuels, fly ash
from thermal plants, cement factories and
asbestos plants.
Harmful effects:
i) They decrease lung function.
ii) They aggravate asthma and cause chronic
bronchitis.
iii) They cause premature death in patients
with heart and lung disease, and an
irregular heart beat.
steps.why: Aerosols are solid particles rather than a gas, so the definition names them as particles first; every effect that follows is then a physical effect of particles lodging in the lungs.
common_mistakes: Calling aerosols a gas. They are solid or liquid PARTICLES dispersed in a gas.
Leaving out the sources. Fly ash, cement and asbestos are the named ones.
steps.memory_tip: Aerosols are dust, not gas: they settle in the lungs, so the effects are lung effects.
steps.margin_note: Definition, sources, then three effects. One mark, so keep the lines short.

steps.label: Noise pollution

lines.text: Noise above 120 dB; damage above 150 dB

lines: Noise pollution is caused by undesirable
high sounds, above 120 dB.
Harmful effects:
i) Extremely high sounds, above 150 dB,
damage the ear drums and cause permanent
hearing impairment.
ii) Noise also causes auditory fatigue,
anxiety, sleeplessness (insomnia) and
stress.
steps.why: The two decibel figures are the whole of this step, so both are given with the effect each one produces. Note that noise is strictly a separate kind of pollution and not a chemical air pollutant; this book lists it sixth among the major air pollutants, so it is answered here as the paper asks.
common_mistakes: Giving only one decibel figure. 120 dB is where noise pollution begins; 150 dB is where damage begins.
Writing that noise pollution only affects hearing. It also causes anxiety, insomnia and stress.
steps.memory_tip: 120 to start, 150 to damage. Two numbers, two lines.
steps.margin_note: Both decibel numbers with their effects. Close the answer here.

insider_note: The six names are worth two marks on their own, so write the numbered list before describing anything — and inside each pollutant the examiner looks for the source line followed by the effects.
